title: The Most Segregated Hour: Why Sunday Morning Is Still Divided
excerpt: The hour we call holy is the hour we keep apart, and the building of that wall has a history older than our discomfort with naming it.
body:
Martin Luther King Jr. said it, and we have been quoting him ever since as if quoting him were the same as repenting. Eleven o'clock on Sunday morning, he said, is the most segregated hour in America. We nod. We put the line on a slide behind the worship leader. Then we drive home to the same neighborhood we drove from, to the same church we have always attended, and nothing about Monday morning is different from Saturday night.

The sociologists confirm what King saw. Michael Emerson and Christian Smith, in their 2000 study Divided by Faith, found that a congregation counts as multiracial only when no single group exceeds eighty percent of the membership, and by that low bar fewer than one in ten American churches qualified. The number has crept upward since. It has not moved far. The most segregated hour is still the most segregated hour, and we have grown comfortable enough with the diagnosis that we no longer feel the wound.

## The Open Door and the Built Preference

There is a serious objection to make here, and I want to make it well before I answer it. Some say the church talks about race too much already, that the constant return to this subject has politicized the pulpit, baptized a partisan agenda, and turned the gospel into a program of social management. They say people of every background already worship freely, that the doors are open, that nobody is turned away, that segregation by preference is not segregation by law and the two should never be confused. They are right about something real. The gospel is not a political platform. A church that preaches a party has lost the cross. And the people who fill our pews on Sunday are not standing at a barred door. No usher checks their skin.

But the open door is not the whole truth, and the people who say it know it is not. Preference did not fall from the sky. Preference was built. The text I want to carry through this is short and it does not flatter us. In Christ, Paul writes, God has broken down the dividing wall of hostility, has made the two groups one, has created in himself one new humanity in place of the two, thus making peace (Ephesians 2:14-15 ESV). Paul is not describing a feeling. He is describing a demolition. There was a wall in the temple, a literal partition past which a Gentile could not go on pain of death, and Paul says the cross tore it down. The question for us is not whether the wall is gone in heaven. The question is who keeps rebuilding it on earth, and the answer includes me.

## A Wall Laid Course by Course

> Preference did not fall from the sky. Preference was built.

Trace it back. The dividing wall in American Christianity was not an accident of geography. In 1845 the Baptists split into North and South over whether a slaveholder could be a missionary, and the Southern Baptist Convention was born to defend a man's right to own a man and call himself sent by God. The Methodists had split the year before. The Presbyterians would fracture too. The largest churches in the land organized themselves around the keeping of human beings as property, and they did it with open Bibles. Jemar Tisby calls this the color of compromise, the long record of a church that did not merely fail to resist racism but actively constructed it (Tisby 2019). The wall in our sanctuaries is the same wall. We did not inherit a neutral silence. We inherited a structure.

After slavery came the next layer. Black Christians who had sat in the balconies of white churches walked out and built their own, not from preference but from refusal, the refusal of white congregations to seat them as equals at the same table. The Black church in America is in large part a monument to white Christian rejection. Then came the federal redlining maps of the 1930s, the restrictive housing covenants, the highways routed through Black neighborhoods, the suburbs sold to whites only. By the time King named it, the segregated hour was the natural fruit of a hundred years of deliberate sorting. We did not choose it on a given Sunday. Our grandparents chose it across a century, and we have not chosen against it.

## The Religion of the Slaveholder

> We did not inherit a neutral silence. We inherited a structure.

Howard Thurman saw the cost from inside. In Jesus and the Disinherited, written in 1949, he asks what the religion of Jesus has to say to those with their backs against the wall, and he records the searing question his own grandmother, born enslaved, put to the faith she was handed. Why would she keep a book that had been used to keep her down. Thurman's answer is that the religion of the slaveholder and the religion of Jesus are not the same religion, that one blesses the wall and the other breaks it (Thurman 1949). The tragedy is that they wore the same name and met in the same hour, and to the watching world they were indistinguishable.

## The Cross Kills the Hostility

Here is the reversal. We treat the segregated hour as a problem of comfort, as if the solution were to make worship a little more varied so everyone feels welcome. But Ephesians does not aim at comfort. The wall Paul names is a wall of hostility, and the cross does not redecorate it. The cross kills the hostility (Ephesians 2:16 ESV). That is violent language and it is meant to be. The thing standing between us is not difference. Difference is the gift of God, every tongue and tribe a facet of his glory. The thing standing between us is enmity, and enmity does not yield to a friendlier greeting at the door. It yields to death, the death of the old humanity that needed the wall to feel safe.

So the law comes before the grace, and the law is this. We built the wall. The white church in America, my church, the tradition I serve in, laid every course of brick with Scripture in hand, and the fact that the mortar has dried and we no longer remember mixing it does not make us innocent. To say the door is open while standing in a building our fathers designed to keep certain people in the balcony is to mistake the absence of a new crime for the presence of repentance. We have not torn down the wall. We have stopped noticing it.

## To Stop Maintaining the Ruin

And here is the grace, which is harder than the comfort we wanted. The cross has already done the demolition. Paul does not command us to build one new humanity. He announces that God has made it, past tense, finished, in the body of Christ. Our task is not construction. It is to stop maintaining the ruin. To walk into the hour we have kept apart and refuse, with our feet and our budgets and our pulpits and our friendships, to keep it apart any longer. That is not a program. It is obedience to something already true.

> The hour is still divided.

King's line was never meant to be a lament we recite. It was meant to be a verdict we answered. We have recited it for sixty years. The hour is still divided. The wall is down in heaven and standing in our sanctuaries, and the hands holding it up are our own.

### Works Cited

Emerson, Michael O., and Christian Smith. Divided by Faith: Evangelical Religion and the Problem of Race in America. New York: Oxford University Press, 2000.

Thurman, Howard. Jesus and the Disinherited. Boston: Beacon Press, 1949.

Tisby, Jemar. The Color of Compromise: The Truth about the American Church's Complicity in Racism. Grand Rapids: Zondervan, 2019.

title: What the Bible Means by Reconciliation
excerpt: We have shrunk a word that once meant the end of a war down to the size of a handshake, and the church is paying for the theft.
body:
A man stands up after the sermon and says he is tired of the word. Reconciliation, he says, has become a code, a Trojan horse, a way to smuggle a politics into the church under the cover of a Bible word. He is not entirely wrong. The word has been used as cover. But the answer to a stolen word is not to abandon it. The answer is to find out what it meant before we got our hands on it.

## A Word Borrowed from War

The Greek is katallage. It does not come from the language of feelings. It comes from the language of war and the language of money, the exchange that ends a hostility, the settling of an account that stood open between two parties who were enemies. When Paul reaches for it, he is not describing two people deciding to get along. He is describing the end of a conflict that one side could not end on its own.

The spine of this is one passage, and I want to press on it the whole way. All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19 ESV). Read it slowly. God is the actor. We were the enemy. The reconciling happens at the cross, where the trespasses that stood between us and God are not waved away but absorbed, not counted, because they are counted somewhere else, in a body on a tree. Reconciliation in the Bible costs blood. It is never cheap. It is never a feeling.

## The Vertical and the Horizontal

> Reconciliation in the Bible costs blood.

Now the strongest objection, and it is strong. Some Christians say that this passage is about reconciliation with God and nothing else, that Paul is writing about salvation, about the sinner brought home, and that to extend it to relations between human groups is to bend a vertical text into a horizontal program it was never meant to carry. They say the gospel is reconciliation with God, full stop, and that when we make it about Black and white we have changed the subject from the cross to a cause. I take this seriously because it guards something precious. The vertical is the foundation. A reconciliation between people that is not grounded in reconciliation with God is just diplomacy, and diplomacy does not save.

But read three verses further than we usually stop. The same Paul who wrote 2 Corinthians 5 wrote that Christ is our peace, who has made the two groups one (Ephesians 2:14 ESV), and the two groups he names are not the sinner and God. They are the Jew and the Gentile, two peoples divided by a wall of hostility, made one in the same cross that reconciled them both to God. Paul does not let us choose between the vertical and the horizontal. He fastens them together. The cross that ends the war with God ends the war between us in the same stroke, because the second war was always a symptom of the first. The wall between peoples is held up by the same pride that built the wall between us and heaven.

## Truth Before Peace

Willie James Jennings traces how we lost this. In The Christian Imagination he argues that the modern church learned to imagine salvation as the rescue of individual souls from the world, severed from bodies, from land, from peoples, and that this severing was not innocent (Jennings 2010). It happened alongside the colonial enterprise, the very moment European Christians were sorting the peoples of the earth by skin and worth. A faith that could reconcile a soul to God while leaving the slave in the field was a faith that had already cut katallage in half. We kept the vertical and amputated the horizontal, and the amputation was convenient. It let us be saved and stay segregated.

> We kept the vertical and amputated the horizontal, and the amputation was convenient.

So what does the full word require. First, it requires truth, because you cannot reconcile an account you refuse to read. The reason God could not count our trespasses against us is that he counted them fully, named them, laid them on Christ. There is no reconciliation that skips the naming of the debt. This is where the church most often fails. We want the peace without the ledger. We want the handshake before the truth. John Perkins, who was beaten nearly to death by Mississippi officers in 1970 and gave his life afterward to the work of Christian community development, insisted that reconciliation without justice is a lie, that you cannot bind a wound you will not first clean (Perkins 1976). The cross did not pretend the debt was small. It paid it in full.

## A Ministry, Not a Feeling

Second, the full word requires that we receive a ministry, not announce a feeling. Paul says God entrusted to us the ministry of reconciliation. A ministry is labor. It has hours and costs and failures. It is not the warm glow of a unity service once a year. It is the slow, expensive, often unrewarded work of a people who have decided that the war is over and now have to live as though it is, in budgets and friendships and the seating of a sanctuary. We were made ministers of the thing God did. That is a job, and most of us have not shown up to it.

## A Peace We Publish, Not Negotiate

> We are not negotiating a peace. We are publishing one.

Here is the reversal we need. We tend to think reconciliation is something we achieve, a goal we work toward, a summit at the end of enough dialogue. But Paul says it is something God already accomplished and then handed to us to announce. We are not negotiating a peace. We are publishing one. The war is over because of the cross, not because of our efforts, and our refusal to live in that peace does not undo it. It only puts us on the wrong side of a verdict already rendered. The reconciled who will not reconcile are a contradiction the watching world can read at a glance.

Lisa Sharon Harper presses the word back to its root in shalom, the Hebrew vision of the world made whole, every relationship set right, between people and God, between people and people, between people and the ground itself (Harper 2016). Reconciliation is not the absence of conflict. It is the presence of that wholeness, the debt settled, the wall down, the enemy seated at the table as kin. That is bigger than getting along, and it is the only thing big enough to be worth the blood it cost.

The man who is tired of the word is tired of a counterfeit, and he should be. The counterfeit is reconciliation without truth, peace without the ledger, a handshake offered to people whose wounds we will not name. But the real word is harder and better than anything we have made of it. It means a war is over because God ended it at terrible cost, and we who were the enemies are now ministers of the peace.

We did not earn this word. We stole it, shrank it, and sold it cheap. The least we can do now is preach it whole.

### Works Cited

Harper, Lisa Sharon. The Very Good Gospel: How Everything Wrong Can Be Made Right. Colorado Springs: WaterBrook, 2016.

Jennings, Willie James. The Christian Imagination: Theology and the Origins of Race. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010.

Perkins, John M. Let Justice Roll Down. Glendale: Regal Books, 1976.

title: The Image of God and the Lie of Race
excerpt: Race is a recent invention dressed up as an ancient fact, and the church helped sew the costume.
body:
Ask a child where race comes from and she will tell you it has always been here, that people simply are these colors and these kinds, the way the sky is blue. Ask a historian and you get a different answer. Race as we mean it, the sorting of humanity into a ladder of worth by the color of skin, is younger than the printing press. It was made. And the making has a date, a motive, and a set of hands, and some of those hands held a Bible.

## The Floor Beneath Every Human

The text I want to carry is the oldest claim Scripture makes about a human being. God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him, male and female he created them (Genesis 1:27 ESV). The imago dei. Before nation, before tribe, before anything we call race, there is this. Every human being bears the image of God, and that image is not distributed by degree. It is not more present in one people and less in another. It is the floor under all of us, the thing that makes a person a person, and Scripture lays it down in the first chapter before sin has even entered the story.

Here is the strong objection, and I want it stated at full strength. Many thoughtful people say the church should stop talking about race entirely, that the very category is the problem, that to keep naming Black and white is to keep alive a fiction we should let die. Color blindness, they argue, is the Christian position. We are all one in Christ, there is neither Jew nor Greek, so why keep sorting the body by a distinction the gospel abolished. There is something genuinely right in this, and I will not pretend otherwise. The category of race is a lie. It has no basis in biology. The differences we have built a ladder upon are surface deep, and the gospel really does make one new humanity out of the many.

## Why Color Blindness Fails

But here is where the color-blind answer fails, and it fails for a reason worth understanding. You cannot heal a wound by refusing to name the weapon. Race is a lie, yes. But it is a lie that built a world, that wrote laws, that drew maps, that decided who got a loan and who got a noose, and you do not undo a four-hundred-year-old structure by closing your eyes to it. Telling a man whose grandfather was redlined out of a neighborhood that you do not see color does not return the house. It only blinds you to why he does not have one. The lie of race must be named precisely because it is a lie that did real damage, and the damage did not vanish when we stopped saying the quiet part out loud.

## The Manufacture of Race

> You cannot heal a wound by refusing to name the weapon.

Trace the invention. Before the European slave trade, people knew themselves by tribe, by city, by faith, by tongue. There were enslaved people of every shade, and slavery, evil as it was, was not yet organized around color. Then came the seventeenth century and a problem the planters needed to solve. African labor was being held for life while European labor was held for years, and that difference needed a justification that could survive a Christian conscience. So the category was built. Willie James Jennings shows how European Christians, in the age of conquest, began to read the peoples of the earth through a new lens, with whiteness placed at the top as the measure of the human and Blackness at the bottom, and how theology lent its weight to the sorting (Jennings 2010). Race was not discovered. It was theologically manufactured to make a sin look like an order of creation.

> Race was not discovered. It was theologically manufactured to make a sin look like an order of creation.

The church did not merely permit this. It supplied the verses. The so-called curse of Ham, drawn from a misreading of Genesis 9, was preached for centuries as the divine charter for African slavery, the claim that a whole people had been cursed to servitude by the word of God. It was a lie laid on top of the lie of race, Scripture twisted to baptize an economy. Esau McCaulley, reading the Bible from within the Black church tradition, shows how the same texts the slaveholder weaponized were read by the enslaved as a charter of dignity and deliverance, how Reading While Black means refusing both the oppressor's distortion and the despair it was meant to produce (McCaulley 2020). The book that was used to forge the chain was the same book that named the prisoner an image-bearer. Only one of those readings was true.

## The Sin Is the Ladder

Here is the reversal, and it is the heart of the matter. We tend to think the problem of race is a problem of difference, that if we could only see past our differences we would be at peace. But Genesis says the opposite. The problem is not that we are different. God made the difference and called the whole creation very good. The problem is that we took a difference God made and built a hierarchy God never authorized. The sin is not color. The sin is the ladder. And the cure for a ladder is not to pretend everyone is on the same rung by ignoring the ranks. The cure is to tear the ladder down and confess we built it.

## The Image as Law and Grace

> The sin is not color. The sin is the ladder.

The imago dei does real work here, and it does it as law before it does it as grace. As law, it indicts. If every human bears the image of God, then every act of the slave trade, every lynching, every redlined map, every sermon that ranked the races was an assault on the image of God, a defacing of his likeness in the person of his neighbor. There is no neutral ground. To diminish a human being by color is to spit on the face of God reflected in that human being, and the church that taught the diminishing taught blasphemy with a Bible open. I am in that church's lineage. So is every white believer in America. The indictment includes us.

And as grace, the imago dei restores. The image cannot be erased by any lie. Four hundred years of teaching that Black bodies were worth less did not make them worth less, because worth was never ours to assign. It was set by God in the first chapter and sealed by God in the incarnation, when the Word took on flesh and dignified the human body forever. Augustine wrote that the image of God in us, defaced by sin, is being renewed in those who turn to Christ, restored to the likeness it was made for (Augustine, The Trinity 14). The lie of race tried to deface the image. The gospel renews it. And a church renewed in the image of God cannot keep the ladder. The renewal and the ladder cannot stand in the same body.

So we do not get color blindness, and we do not get the ladder either. We get something harder than both. We get the call to name the lie for what it is, to confess the hands that made it, and to look at every human face, including the faces our fathers ranked, and see what was always there.

The image of God. Defaced for four centuries. Never once erased.

### Works Cited

Augustine. The Trinity. Translated by Edmund Hill. Brooklyn: New City Press, 1991.

Jennings, Willie James. The Christian Imagination: Theology and the Origins of Race. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2010.

McCaulley, Esau. Reading While Black: African American Biblical Interpretation as an Exercise in Hope. Downers Grove: InterVarsity Press, 2020.

title: Lament: The Prayer the Church Forgot
excerpt: We taught ourselves to skip past the prayers of grief, and in skipping them we lost the only language honest enough to carry what race has done.
body:
Open the hymnal of most white churches and try to find a song that does not resolve. Try to find one that ends in the question and not the answer, that leaves the grief standing, that does not hurry to the bridge where everything is fine. You will be looking a long time. We have a thousand songs of triumph and almost none of sorrow, and that absence is not a matter of taste. It is a theology, and it has cost us the ability to speak honestly about race.

## The Prayers That Do Not Resolve

> Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith refusing to lie about the state of the world.

A full third of the Psalms are laments, prayers of complaint, grief, and protest addressed to God. They are not polite. How long, O Lord. Will you forget me forever (Psalm 13:1 ESV). My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Psalm 22:1 ESV). These are not the prayers of people whose faith is failing. They are the prayers of the most faithful people in the Bible, and Jesus himself died with one of them on his lips. Lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith refusing to lie about the state of the world.

Let me carry one psalm as the spine. Psalm 13 moves in three movements, and the church has learned to live only in the last. It opens in complaint, four times the cry how long, the prayer of a man who feels forgotten by the God he still addresses. Then it turns to petition, consider and answer me, light up my eyes. And only at the end does it arrive at trust, I will sing to the Lord because he has dealt bountifully with me (Psalm 13:6 ESV). Three movements. Complaint, petition, trust. We skip the first two and sing only the third, and a third of a prayer is not a prayer. It is a performance of arrival we have not actually made.

## Grief as the Road to Hope

Now the strong objection, because there is one. Some will say that lament risks becoming a wallow, that endless grief over race keeps wounds open that grace means to close, that the gospel calls us to rejoice and to forgive and to look forward, not to camp in lamentation as if the resurrection had not happened. They say a faith fixated on sorrow has forgotten the empty tomb. And there is truth here worth holding. The Christian does not grieve as one without hope. Lament that never moves toward trust curdles into despair, and despair is not a Christian word.

But notice what the objection assumes. It assumes that the choice is between grief and hope, when the Psalms refuse that choice entirely. Psalm 13 does not arrive at trust by skipping the complaint. It arrives at trust through the complaint, by way of it, having spoken the grief fully to God first. The hope at the end of the psalm is earned, weighted, real, precisely because the sorrow at the beginning was not censored. A church that cannot lament cannot truly hope either, because its hope has never passed through honesty. It has only passed around it. And a hope that goes around the wound is a denial wearing the mask of faith.

## The Liturgical Failure of the White Church

Here is where this touches race directly. The reason the white church struggles to speak about race is, in part, a liturgical failure. We have no language for it. We know how to celebrate and we know how to instruct, but we do not know how to grieve, because we deleted grief from our worship generations ago. So when the history of slavery and lynching and segregation is set before us, we have no vessel to receive it. We reach for explanation, for defense, for the quick turn to reconciliation, because we never learned the prayer that simply sits in the wreckage and says to God, how long. The Black church kept that prayer. The spirituals were lament, the slave singing nobody knows the trouble I have seen straight into the face of God. We who lost lament lost the very language the moment required.

## The Lynchings We Never Mourned

> We never even learned to cry about it.

The history is specific and the silence around it is the proof. From 1877 to 1950 the historians at the Equal Justice Initiative have documented more than four thousand racial terror lynchings in the American South, public killings often attended by churchgoing crowds, sometimes on a Sunday, sometimes with the body displayed near a house of worship. The white church of that era did not lament these murders. It largely watched, or looked away, or in some cases supplied the crowd. There is no widely sung hymn of grief for them. The absence of that lament, eighty years on, is itself a sin we have not confessed. We never even learned to cry about it.

Walter Brueggemann argues that the loss of lament is the loss of a whole dimension of faith, that a community which can only praise has surrendered its capacity to hold God accountable and to tell the truth about its own pain (Brueggemann 1986). Without lament, he says, the covenant becomes one-sided, a relationship in which the powerful are never questioned and the suffering are never heard. A church that cannot lament cannot do justice, because justice begins with the truthful naming of what is wrong, and that naming, addressed to God, is exactly what lament is. We traded the prayer for a smile, and we lost the truth in the trade.

## Lament as Intimacy

Here is the reversal. We have treated lament as a sign of weak faith, a stage to grow out of, a sorrow that mature believers transcend. But the Bible treats lament as a sign of intimacy. You do not complain to a stranger. You complain to a father, to the one you trust enough to be honest with, to the one you believe is listening and able. The freedom to cry how long, O Lord is the freedom of a child who knows the father is there. To refuse lament is not strength. It is distance. It is a politeness that has stopped believing God can take the truth.

> A church too proud to grieve is a church that thinks itself above its own Lord.

The cross does the deepest work here, and it does it before it comforts. On the cross Jesus prayed Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and in praying it he sanctified lament forever. God himself, in the flesh, lamented. The sinless one took the prayer of grief onto his own lips and made it holy. So there is no spiritual height above lament, because the highest one stooped into it. The law here is plain. A church too proud to grieve is a church that thinks itself above its own Lord.

And the grace is this. Because Christ lamented and was heard, our laments are heard too. The how long is not a cry into an empty sky. It rises to a God who has himself cried it, who knows the weight of the forsaken from the inside, who will not despise the broken prayer because he prayed it first. We are free to grieve all the way down, because the bottom is not despair. The bottom is a man on a cross who got there before us.

We forgot how to lament, and forgetting it, we lost the only honest language we had for what race has done. The first repentance may be smaller and harder than we think. Not a program. A prayer. How long, O Lord. We have not even begun to pray it.

### Works Cited

Brueggemann, Walter. The Costly Loss of Lament. Journal for the Study of the Old Testament 36 (1986): 57-71.

Equal Justice Initiative. Lynching in America: Confronting the Legacy of Racial Terror. Montgomery: Equal Justice Initiative, 2017.

Thurman, Howard. Jesus and the Disinherited. Boston: Beacon Press, 1949.

title: Building the Multiethnic Church Without Faking It
excerpt: A church can put many colors in the room and still leave one culture in charge of everything, and God is not fooled by the photograph.
body:
There is a kind of multiethnic church that exists mostly in the brochure. The faces on the website are varied. The worship band is varied. The greeters at the door were chosen, you suspect, with the camera in mind. And underneath the varied surface, every decision that matters is made by one group, in one cultural key, in the style they have always preferred, and the people of other backgrounds are welcome to attend the church that white leadership has built. This is not the one new humanity of Ephesians. It is assimilation with a diversity filter, and the people being assimilated can feel the difference even when the brochure cannot.

## The Church in the Brochure

The question this article asks is not whether to build a multiethnic church. The question is how to build one that is real, and the difference between the real and the fake is not the photograph. It is who holds the power.

> It is assimilation with a diversity filter, and the people being assimilated can feel the difference even when the brochure cannot.

The spine is a scene from the early church, the first time the gospel had to decide whether it was big enough to hold more than one culture. In Acts 6 the church in Jerusalem is feeding its widows, and a complaint arises. The Hellenists, the Greek-speaking Jews, find that their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution, while the Hebrew-speaking majority's widows are cared for (Acts 6:1 ESV). A diverse church. A real grievance from the minority culture. And here is what the apostles do not do. They do not tell the Hellenists they are imagining it. They do not call for unity over division. They restructure the leadership. They appoint seven men to oversee the distribution, and every single name on the list is Greek. The minority that was overlooked is given the power to fix the problem. That is how the first multiethnic church handled it, and it should haunt every church that handles it differently.

## When the Minority Is Overlooked

Now the strong objection. Some will say this whole project is misguided, that churches grow best when they reach a particular people with a particular culture, that the homogeneous unit principle, named by church-growth researchers in the 1970s, is simply realism, that people come to faith most readily among their own kind, and that forcing a multiethnic blend produces awkward, shrinking congregations while letting churches be culturally specific produces thriving ones. There is data behind this, and I will not wave it away. It is often true that the single-culture church grows faster. The multiethnic church is harder, slower, and more prone to conflict. Anyone who tells you otherwise has not tried it.

## A Faster Church That Denies the Cross

But here is where the realism fails. The gospel was never a growth strategy. The dividing wall in Ephesians was not torn down because mixed congregations grow better. It was torn down because Christ died to make the two one, and a church that stays segregated for the sake of efficiency has subordinated the cross to the numbers. Paul could have grown the church in Antioch faster by keeping Jews and Gentiles in separate fellowships. Instead he confronted Peter to his face when Peter pulled back from the Gentile table (Galatians 2:11-14 ESV), because the unity of the body across the dividing line was not optional decoration. It was the truth of the gospel itself, visible. A faster church that contradicts the cross is not a success. It is a well-attended denial.

So how is it built without faking it. First, power must move, not just bodies. The Acts 6 pattern is not diversity in the pews. It is diversity in the decisions. A church that wants people of color in the room but keeps every position of real authority in white hands has built a plantation with better music. The test is not the photo on Sunday. The test is who sets the budget, who chooses the preaching, who shapes the worship, whose cultural instincts are treated as normal and whose are treated as additions. Until that power is genuinely shared, the multiethnic church is a costume.

## Power Must Move, Not Just Bodies

> A church that wants people of color in the room but keeps every position of real authority in white hands has built a plantation with better music.

Second, one culture cannot be the default. In the fake version, the dominant culture's way of doing everything is simply the water, invisible, assumed, and every other culture is an accommodation to be tolerated on special Sundays. The real version dies to that. It means the majority gives up the comfort of its own preferences as the unquestioned norm, in music, in length, in volume, in the rhythm of the service, in the very feel of belonging. This is a death, and it is felt as a death by those asked to die. The white believer who has never once worshiped in a style not built for him is being asked to lose something he did not know he had. That losing is the cross at work in the body, and there is no real multiethnic church without it.

John Perkins spent his life on this and refused the cheap version. Reconciliation, he insisted, is not Black and white people smiling in a sanctuary. It is the redistribution of power and resources, the relocation of the comfortable into the hard places, the redistribution that makes the unity more than a feeling (Perkins 1976). His three R's, relocation, reconciliation, redistribution, put the costly word last and meant it. A church that wants the reconciliation without the redistribution wants the photograph without the cost, and Perkins, who bled for this, would not let us have it on those terms.

Here is the reversal. We tend to think the multiethnic church is a goal we build, a thing we assemble by careful planning, the right hires and the right music and the right outreach. But Ephesians says the one new humanity is not something we build. It is something Christ already made, on the cross, finished. Which means our task is not construction but excavation. We are not assembling a unity that does not exist. We are removing the rubble, the structures and habits and power arrangements, that bury a unity Christ already accomplished. The church does not manufacture the new humanity. It stops smothering it.

## Excavation, Not Construction

And this is where law precedes grace one more time. The law: the segregated church and the cosmetically diverse church are both denials of a unity that already exists in Christ, and no amount of good intention changes the denial into obedience. To leave the power where it has always been while claiming the name of reconciliation is to lie with a budget. That is the indictment, and as a white pastor I stand inside it, because the default culture of my tradition is the one I have most often mistaken for the gospel itself.

The grace: because the new humanity is Christ's accomplishment and not ours, we are not condemned to build what we cannot build. The pressure is off our cleverness and onto his finished work. We are freed to do the slow, costly, unglamorous labor of clearing rubble, knowing the thing underneath is real, already there, waiting to be uncovered. The multiethnic church is not a goal we might fail to reach. It is a fact we are called to stop hiding.

So the brochure is the wrong question. The right question is the one the Hellenist widows asked without words. When the minority is overlooked, who gets the power to fix it. Answer that honestly, and you will know whether you have built the one new humanity or only its photograph.

> God is not looking at the picture. He is reading the ledger of who decides.

God is not looking at the picture. He is reading the ledger of who decides.
